Fleet guide

Fleet management, explained

A plain-language primer for new fleet managers, program leads and the finance staff who work with them.

On this page

What it is What a fleet manager does Where telematics fits Metrics that matter Policy and compliance Where to start

What is fleet management?

Fleet management is the work of acquiring, assigning, operating, maintaining and disposing of an organization's vehicles so they support its mission at the lowest reasonable cost and risk. A fleet can be ten pickup trucks or ten thousand sedans, buses and specialty vehicles. The discipline is the same: know what you have, know how it is used, and make each vehicle earn its place.

What does a fleet manager do?

Day to day, a fleet manager keeps vehicles available and safe. Over the year, the job is mostly decisions and paperwork:

  • Matching vehicle type and count to actual mission requirements
  • Planning replacements and budgeting for lease, fuel and maintenance
  • Tracking utilization and justifying vehicles that fall short
  • Keeping the inventory accurate and reconciled to finance records
  • Meeting reporting deadlines and responding to audits and data calls

Where does telematics fit?

A telematics device reports a vehicle's location, engine hours, mileage, idling and diagnostic codes. It replaces odometer estimates with measured use. On its own it answers "where and how much." Joined with fuel, maintenance, lease and assignment records, it answers the questions leadership asks: which vehicles do we need, what do they cost, and are we following policy.

Telematics does not decide anything by itself. A vehicle parked all week might be idle waste or an emergency-response asset doing exactly its job. The policy, not the device, defines what counts as utilized.

Metrics that matter

A short set of measures covers most decisions. What matters is using the same definitions every period.

MetricWhat it tells youTypical source
Utilizationmi · hrs · daysWhether a vehicle is used enough to justify keeping itTelematics, odometer readings, trip logs
Idle time% of engine-onFuel burned while not moving; a driver-behavior and cost signalTelematics
Cost per mile$ / miTotal cost of operation, comparable across vehicle typesLease, fuel card, maintenance systems
Fuel economympg · mpgeEfficiency against the vehicle class; flags misuse or mechanical issuesFuel card joined to mileage
PM compliance% on timeWhether preventive maintenance happens before breakdownsMaintenance records, diagnostic codes
Age and replacementyrs · miWhich vehicles are due, and what replacement will costInventory, replacement standards

Policy and compliance

Public fleets operate under written rules, and a decision that is not traceable to policy rarely survives review. For federal agencies, the core references include:

  • 41 CFR Part 102-34: GSA's Federal Management Regulation for motor vehicle management
  • FAST (Federal Automotive Statistical Tool): the annual reporting of federal fleet inventory, cost, fuel use and budget projections
  • EPAct 2005 §701: the requirement that federal dual-fueled vehicles use alternative fuel unless a waiver applies

State and local governments set their own fleet and take-home vehicle policies, often shaped by audits. Commercial fleets answer to safety regulators, insurers and their own finance teams. In every case the pattern holds: write down the rule, measure against it, and keep the evidence.

Where to start

Pick one location or one vehicle class. Pull 90 days of telematics and a current inventory, agree on the utilization definition, and look at the bottom quarter of the list. That single view usually pays for the next step.

FAQ

Common questions

Do we need to buy new telematics devices?

Usually not. We work with the telematics provider you already use and with exports from fuel card, maintenance and lease systems. If you have no telematics yet, we help you scope what to collect before you buy.

What data do you need to get started?

A current vehicle inventory with assignments, and 90 days of usage data. Telematics exports are ideal; odometer readings or trip logs work for a first pass. Fuel and maintenance records sharpen the cost picture.

How long does a first utilization review take?

For a single location or vehicle class with clean exports, a baseline review is typically a few weeks. We scope the timeline with you once we see the data.

Who owns the dashboards and analysis?

You do. Models, dashboards and documentation are delivered in your environment, with a written method so your staff can maintain them.

How do you handle our data?

We work within your systems and security requirements wherever possible, collect only the fields the analysis needs, and return or delete working copies at the end of the engagement.

Do you work with public agencies?

Yes. Public-sector fleets are our focus: state and local governments and federal civilian agencies, alongside commercial fleets.
